title: Ranveer Brar's Tandoori Corn Chaat Turns an Evening Snack Spicy
excerpt: Celebrity chef Ranveer Brar's step-by-step tandoori corn chaat dresses sweet corn in a spiced curd marinade, chars it, and finishes it chaat-style — a smoky upgrade to the classic evening snack.
body:
• Chef Ranveer Brar has shared a step-by-step tandoori corn chaat recipe, giving the classic evening snack a smoky, spice-forward upgrade.
  • The preparation hinges on a thick-curd tandoori marinade — Kashmiri red chilli, turmeric, coriander and cumin powders, garam masala, ginger-garlic paste and lemon juice — with a short rest before cooking.
  • The marinated corn is roasted on a hot tawa, in an oven or in an air fryer, brushed with butter until lightly charred, then finished chaat-style.
  • A final toss of chaat masala, fresh coriander and lemon juice keeps it firmly street food: tangy, fiery and served piping hot.

Celebrity chef Ranveer Brar has given one of India's favourite evening snacks a tandoori twist. According to Hindustan Times, the chef shared a step-by-step recipe for tandoori corn chaat — a dish that takes sweet corn, dresses it in a spiced curd marinade, chars it over high heat and finishes it the way any proper chaat deserves: with chaat masala, fresh coriander and a squeeze of lemon.

The idea lands at the right moment. Corn — bhutta — is as much a mood as it is an ingredient, tied to rainy evenings and roadside stalls. Brar's version borrows the tandoori playbook usually reserved for paneer and chicken and applies it to something far simpler, turning a humble cob of corn into a snack with real swagger.

The marinade does the heavy lifting

The heart of the recipe is a tandoori-style marinade built on thick curd, according to published versions of the preparation. Kashmiri red chilli powder brings the colour, turmeric and coriander powder bring the base, cumin powder and garam masala bring the warmth, and ginger-garlic paste and lemon juice bring the bite. The corn — typically boiled first — is coated in this mixture and left to rest for about 15 to 20 minutes so the spices settle into the kernels.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=5PWIG-OVaNc

Cooking is where the tandoor effect comes in. Without a clay oven, the corn goes onto a hot tawa, into a hot oven or into an air fryer, brushed with butter, and roasted until lightly charred at the edges. That charring is non-negotiable — it is what separates tandoori-style corn from plain boiled corn tossed in masala. The final flourish is pure chaat: a dusting of chaat masala, chopped fresh coriander and lemon juice, served immediately while hot.

Brar's own recipe archive shows the same instincts at work in other corn preparations. His corn chaat method starts with pressure-cooking corn on the cob with dry red chillies, ginger, coriander roots, cinnamon, black cardamom and peppercorns before tossing the kernels with onion, tomato, green chillies, black salt and chaat masala. The through-line is consistent: treat the corn with respect, layer the spices, finish fresh.

Why corn chaat keeps winning

Corn chaat endures because it is one of the rare snacks that is cheap, fast and forgiving. Frozen corn is available year-round, the spice cabinet does the rest, and the whole thing comes together in roughly half an hour. The monsoon-season corn chaat playbook — stir-frying blanched kernels until golden, then tossing with roasted cumin, black salt, lemon and ginger juice — works with whatever vegetables are on hand.

There is also the health argument, which matters to the evening-snack crowd trying to dodge the biscuit tin. Corn brings fibre to the plate, and a tandoori-style preparation uses a curd-based marinade and a hot surface rather than a deep fryer. It is indulgence-adjacent without the guilt spiral — the four-o'clock hunger fix that still lets dinner happen.

A diaspora-friendly tandoor

For the Indian diaspora, this recipe travels well. Sweet corn is a supermarket staple in the US, the marinade uses spices most Indian kitchens abroad already stock, and an air fryer or broiler stands in convincingly for the roadside coal grill. It is the kind of recipe that recreates a very specific Indian feeling — the smoky bhutta of a rainy evening — with equipment already sitting on the counter.

What's next

Home cooks can treat Brar's version as a template rather than a rulebook: keep the curd marinade and the char, then improvise the finish. A pinch of black salt deepens the tang, a little butter brushed on at the end adds richness, and anyone chasing extra heat can push the Kashmiri chilli further. The only real instruction is the one chaat has always carried — serve it hot, and don't wait.
